示范在专家轨迹沿线给出低不确定性的奖励估计，但会留下大片状态空间区域”欠确定”（underdetermined）； 成对偏好提供更广的覆盖，但可能把较高的奖励赋给那些被频繁访问、却并非全局最优的中间状态； 评分能可靠地识别出目标状态，但对其周围奖励地形的信息有限； 停止信号强烈约束不安全或低奖励区域，但在”避开之外什么行为是值得要的”这一点上提供相对较少的指引。
这些局限恰好说明了不同反馈类型的互补本质——当它们被组合时，上述局限得以缓解。我们基于组合反馈训练的奖励模型能够以很高的保真度重建原始的真实奖励函数，并可靠地同时识别高奖励与低奖励状态。 6.2 组合反馈提升策略性能与奖励识别（Combining Feedback Improves Policy Performance and Reward Identification）我们在 [表 1]（原文第 8 页，跨栏表格）中评估不同反馈组合在一系列网格世界与连续控制环境中的下游策略性能。对每种组合，我们都针对学习到的奖励估计优化一个策略，并报告该策略关于真实奖励函数的总回报。 所有结果在 10 次运行上取平均；回报按环境线性缩放，使得 100 对应于用真实奖励训练出的近似最优策略的性能，0 对应于均匀随机策略的回报。因此，超过 100 的数值表示学习策略优于用真实奖励训练的策略。虽然这些归一化指标刻画了下游策略性能，但它们并不整体反映奖励恢复的质量。为此，我们还报告 EPIC 距离（Gleave et al., 2021）：对仅在基于势的塑形（potential-based shaping）、正缩放与常数平移意义下等价的奖励函数，EPIC 距离为 0。我们只在可精确比较奖励的表格型环境中报告 EPIC 距离。 [表 1] 说明：主表分为上下两部分——上部分为”归一化平均回报（越高越好）”，下部分为”平均 EPIC 距离（越低越好）”，环境行依次为 grid_cliff、grid_sparse、grid_trap、Acrobot-v1、CartPole-v1、LunarLander-v3；列对应各种单模态与多模态反馈组合（深灰底为最优，浅灰底为次优）。原文表格位于第 8 页，请对照原 PDF 查看逐列数值。 组合全部反馈类型获得最强的整体性能。 总体上，PDR（偏好＋示范＋评分等组合）在各环境中表现强劲，在 6 个环境中的 4 个取得最好或接近最好的性能，例外是 Acrobot-v1 与 LunarLander-v3。这支持我们的核心假设：MAVRL 能够利用不同反馈类型中包含的互补信息。 没有任何单一类型基线在所有环境中占优。 或许并不令人意外：示范（D）在稀疏奖励设置中表现出色——例如 grid_sparse（95.0）与 LunarLander-v3（115.7）；评分（R）在 CartPole-v1 的单一反馈方法中表现最好（100）。偏好（P）作为独立模态表现相对温和，但在与其他模态组合时贡献显著——这与以往”成对比较需要大量样本才能达到有竞争力的性能”的发现一致（Christiano et al., 2017）。 停止反馈与其他反馈互补。 在若干环境中，包含停止反馈的组合通常优于不含停止反馈的对应组合。例如在 grid_sparse 中，加入停止反馈的组合（100.0）优于仅用示范 D（95.0）；含停止反馈的偏好组合（70.6）也优于仅偏好（58.8）。这说明停止信号提供了关于轨迹次优性的宝贵信息，而这种信息很难从其他反馈中获取。 EPIC 距离揭示策略性能之外的奖励恢复质量。 在计算 EPIC 的三个表格型环境中，PDR 取得最低（grid_cliff：0.481；grid_trap：0.520）或次低（grid_sparse：0.383）的 EPIC 距离。EPIC 与性能的偏差只出现在 grid_sparse 上：某一组合达到最低 EPIC（0.380）却只有中等的策略性能（82.3），这表明”忠实的奖励恢复”与”较高的下游性能”虽不完全等价，但通过组合所有反馈模态可以同时实现。 相对非变分基线，MAVRL 既有效又高效。 [表 2]（原文第 8 页底部）把 MAVRL 与两种自然的替代方法对比：
MCMC：一种非摊销的贝叶斯奖励学习方法，代表后验推断的”金标准”； 事后奖励平均（Post-Hoc Reward Averaging）：一种非变分启发式，通过集成平均组合多个独立训练的奖励估计（参见 Metz et al., 2025）。

图中奖励模型与基线都在未扰动设定下训练并在整个变化过程中保持固定。可以观察到：在网格环境中，由多类型反馈推断的奖励训练出的策略在扰动下比由单一反馈模态或仅靠模仿训练的策略衰减得更平缓。虽然组合反馈的下游性能仍比模仿基线衰减得更平缓，但某些单模态（例如 R）的性能反而超过它——这与未扰动设定下的情况一致。在网格世界中，动作随机性增大导致模仿与单反馈奖励模型（例如 R、P、D）快速恶化，而从组合反馈学到的奖励能保持更高的平均回报。Acrobot-v1 中也有类似模式：系统动力学的结构性变化对模仿策略与单反馈奖励模型的冲击不成比例地大，而组合反馈在各级扰动下给出持续更稳定的性能。在 LunarLander-v3 中，重力与风扰动严重削弱了 BC 的性能；相比之下，MAVRL——尤其是用多类型反馈（PDR）和示范反馈（D）训练时——在越来越有挑战性的动力学下依然显著更鲁棒。 多类型反馈能补偿大多数被错误设定的模态。 接下来我们检验多类型优势能否延伸到”反馈信号本身被污染”的情形——采用与第 6.2 节相同的固定分配反馈预算。我们施加四种错误设定（分别或联合）：低估偏好（）与示范（）的标注者理性程度、在评分效用上加性高斯噪声、以及停止倾向被误校准。grid_cliff 与 grid_sparse 的结果见 [表 3]（原文第 9 页；grid_trap 上的同样结论见表 5）。 [表 3] 说明：上半部分为单模态模型，下半部分为使用完整反馈集合的 MAVRL；每一行把指定通道的数据侧参数破坏掉，而模型仍假设其取值完好（被破坏的模态在原表中以模糊/灰色标出，例如 PDRS 表示偏好被错误设定）。列含义：Base＝完好设定的归一化回报；Misspec.＝均值±标准误；Rat.＝Misspec./Base。原文数值请对照原 PDF。 两点观察很突出。第一，在四种污染中的三种（偏好、评分与停止）下，PDR 保留了其完好设定性能的 ≥90%，而相应的单模态基线则崩塌到低至 0.10 的比例。这表明存在很强的补偿效应：在多个反馈类型上的联合推断吸收来自单一来源的污染，而不是把它传播开。第二，例外是示范：污染示范把 PDR 打到 0.38–0.50 的比例；同时污染全部四个通道也大致达到同一水平（0.43–0.50）。因此 PDR 的最坏情况退化受限于示范通道，而不是在各通道之间叠加恶化。总体而言，多类型优势可延伸到四个反馈通道中三个的上游污染场景，而示范仍是结构性的薄弱点。
7. 结论（Conclusion）本文将”从多类型反馈学习奖励”表述为对共享潜在奖励函数的贝叶斯推断：每种反馈模态都通过显式似然作出贡献。我们提出了 MAVRL——一种可扩展的摊销变分推断算法，它优化单一统一目标。经验上我们发现：不同反馈类型会诱导出不同的奖励与不确定性结构，而从多个模态联合推断奖励能够利用它们的互补优势，从而提升奖励恢复、下游策略性能与鲁棒性。 局限性（Limitations）。 我们的评估局限于仿真环境——虽然这允许对不同类型的反馈做受控分析，但并未捕捉真实世界任务的完整复杂性。此外，我们依赖合成生成的反馈；把 MAVRL 应用到可能表现出系统性偏差、不一致或依赖上下文的判断的真实人类反馈，仍是未来工作的重要方向。最后，尽管我们的框架能推断奖励不确定性，我们尚未利用这种不确定性来引导反馈采集，因此把异质反馈的主动学习（active learning）留作一个有前景的未来方向。

附录（Appendix）附录 A 实现细节（Implementation Details）A.1 模型结构（Model Architecture）奖励编码器 与 Q 值估计器 都实现为两层 MLP，激活函数为 Leaky ReLU。对于网格环境，使用学习率 、批大小 32，奖励只依赖状态：。对于控制任务（CartPole-v1、Acrobot-v1、LunarLander-v3），使用学习率 、批大小 128，奖励依赖状态–动作对：。所有模型都用带梯度裁剪（最大范数 1.0）的 AdamW 训练（Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019）。奖励编码器参数化一个以标准正态分布为先验的高斯后验，并用重参数化技巧训练。专家参考策略用 Stable-Baselines3 的 DQN（LunarLander-v3 以外）与 PPO（LunarLander-v3）训练（Raffin et al., 2021）。 超参数优化。 对每个环境与反馈组合，用 Optuna 的多元 TPE 采样器（constant_liar=True，20 个启动试验）调优超参数（Akiba et al., 2019）。每个试验在采样配置下、跨多个随机种子训练模型，并按所选验证指标打分。联合搜索空间包括：
损失权重 与 ，在 上对数均匀采样； 奖励编码器宽度：网格为每层 16 / 32 / 64 个隐单元，控制任务为 64 / 128 / 256； 奖励模型优化器：学习率（对数均匀 ）、批大小（网格为 16 / 32 / 64 / 128，控制任务为 32 / 64 / 128 / 256）； 对 LunarLander-v3，还包括 PPO 重训的超参数（学习率、裁剪范围、熵/价值系数、GAE-、梯度范数上界等）。
调优在两种”反馈分配模式”下进行：
等预算（Dirichlet）模式：把固定的总反馈预算通过平坦-Dirichlet 分配（由 Optuna 建议）切分到各个激活模态。每种模态设置上限（例如网格/控制任务分别 ≤16/≤32 条示范，因为示范似然会很快饱和），通过裁剪 Dirichlet 比例并重新分配超出的部分来实施。 固定分配模式：每个模态被分配规定的样本数（FIXED_SAMPLE_COUNTS），只搜索上述优化超参数。该模式用于在”有用且可比”的预算下刻画每个模态的贡献，而不与分配选择相混淆。
对同一环境内的所有方法统一施加相同的调优协议（采样器、搜索空间、每试验种子数、验证指标），从而保证所报数字反映的是匹配计算量下的最佳搜索性能。模型与训练代码基于 PyTorch 实现（Paszke et al., 2019）。 A.2 反馈模拟（Feedback Simulation）我们用温度参数为 的 Boltzmann 理性策略 rollout 收集轨迹，并从中模拟人类反馈。下面给出各类反馈的生成过程。 偏好（Preferences）。 从收集到的轨迹中随机提取固定长度 的片段。对每对片段 ，计算其归一化回报 ，并按 Bradley–Terry 模型生成一个偏好：
其中 表示 logistic sigmoid， 控制偏好理性程度。观测偏好按该概率作为 Bernoulli 随机变量采样。取值： ；片段长度 （网格）或 （其余环境）；轨迹理性 （网格，均匀策略）或 （其余环境）。 示范（Demonstrations）。 专家示范通过 rollout Boltzmann 理性策略 生成，其中 为最优 Q 函数。示范理性 控制专家最优程度。取值： （网格）， （其余所有环境）。 评分（Ratings）。 从轨迹中提取随机片段并计算其归一化回报。切点 放在逐步片段回报的 百分位处。随后在累积 logit 模型下随机采样评分：
该式产生近似均衡的类别。典型参数： 个类别，片段长度 （网格；其余环境），轨迹理性 （分别对应网格、Acrobot-v1 与 CartPole-v1、LunarLander-v3）。 停止信号（Stops）。 用基于累积遗憾的离散时间风险模型模拟停止反馈。对一条轨迹片段，在每个时间步计算瞬时遗憾 ，并维护一个折扣累积遗憾：
其中 是遗憾折扣因子，控制过去次优性被”遗忘”的速度。风险率（给定此前未停止时在时刻 停止的概率）为
灵敏度参数 从数据校准为 ，其中 是缩放常数， 是参考遗憾水平（通常取所有片段最大累积遗憾的第 50 百分位）。 越大，停止行为越激进。停止时间顺序采样：在每个时间步 以概率 采样一个停止事件；若片段内没有停止发生，则观测右删失。参数： ，遗憾折扣 ，参考百分位 50%，片段长度 （网格；其余环境），轨迹理性 。 附录 B 硬件与计算资源（Hardware and Computational Resources）由于第 6 节要评估大量配置，单个奖励模型的训练与评估运行被分发到由 SLURM 管理的机构集群上，每个 worker 分配 4 个 CPU 核与 8 GB 内存。由于奖励编码器与 Q 值估计器网络很小，无需 GPU 加速。最终实验总计算量约为 CPU·小时。 需要说明的是，在单机上，单次奖励模型训练大约耗时：网格环境 2 分钟，其余环境约 15 分钟；其中大部分计算时间花在”用推断出的奖励函数重训策略以进行评估”上。 附录 C 等预算结果（Equal Budget Results）对每个环境，我们固定一个总反馈预算 ，由等预算表中的全部 11 个模态子集共享：四种反馈各自单独使用（P、D、R、S）、全部六种两两组合，以及四者的完整组合（PDRS）。预算为：三个表格型网格（grid_cliff、grid_sparse、grid_trap）、Acrobot-v1 与 CartPole-v1 取 个样本；LunarLander-v3 取 个样本。 对每一对（环境，模态子集），我们运行一次独立的 TPE（Tree-structured Parzen Estimator）搜索，联合调节 (i) 分配给每个激活反馈类型的比例，以及 (ii) 奖励模型的训练超参数（编码器大小、学习率、批大小、重要性加权开关、KL 权重、TD 权重）；对非表格环境，搜索还额外调节下游 PPO 重训超参数。每个试验在表格环境下用 20 个随机种子、非表格环境下用 10 个随机种子训练奖励模型，并按”逐种子归一化折扣回报均值”（表格）或”平均回合回报”（非表格）打分；每个研究运行 125–200 个试验。最佳试验的奖励模型 checkpoint 就是本文所有下游迁移与误设实验所使用的那一批。 [表 4] 位置与内容说明：原文第 15 页。该表给出等预算设定下、跨环境的各反馈组合的归一化平均回报与平均 EPIC 距离（ ）。表结构同表 1（上半部分为回报、下半部分为 EPIC，越低越好）。回报按环境归一化，100 对应真实奖励训练出的近似最优策略、0 对应均匀随机策略；深灰底为该环境最优（回报在 1% 以内），浅灰底为该区间外次优。具体数值请对照原 PDF。 附录 D 完整误设结果（Full Misspecification Results）我们考虑四种误设变体，可单独或联合施加：
偏好：低估标注者噪声—— 而模型假设 ； 示范：同样低估标注者噪声—— 而模型假设 ；
（上述两者都表示：数据在高度含噪标注下生成，而模型假设标注者近乎理性。）
评分：在评分分配之前给片段效用叠加高斯噪声 ，而模型假设效用无噪声； 停止倾向：误校准—— 而模型假设 。
在所有情况下，奖励模型都用与主表相同的、良好设定的参数训练，因此未扰动基线不变。 [表 5] 位置与内容说明：原文第 15 页（表 3 的补全版，包含 grid_trap 一列）。表结构同表 3：上为单模态模型，下为完整反馈集合的 MAVRL；每行破坏指定通道的数据侧参数，被破坏的模态在原表中以模糊方式标出（例如 PDRS 表示偏好被误设）。列：Base（完好设定归一化回报）、Misspec.（均值±标准误）、Rat.（=Misspec./Base）。正文第 6.3 节所述规律在 grid_trap 上同样成立，具体数值请对照原 PDF。 附录 E 额外迁移结果与扰动详细描述（Additional Transfer Results and Detailed Perturbation Description）所有反馈组合的迁移性能结果见 [图 3]（原文第 17 页）。 [图 3] 内容说明（中文）：该图展示三种动力学扰动场景下、由各方法推断的奖励训练出的策略的归一化平均回报（ ）。奖励模型与基线在未扰动设定下训练、并在整个变化过程中保持固定。图 (a)(b) 分别对应 grid_cliff 与 grid_trap 中”环境随机性”（0→0.8）的逐步增强；(c) 为 Acrobot-v1 摆杆两段长度之比的增大（约 1.0→2.0）；(d) 为 LunarLander-v3 重力与风力的增强。回报按”未扰动设定下用真实奖励训练出的近似最优策略＝100.0、均匀随机策略＝0.0”归一化，误差棒为标准误。各曲线对应本文全部单模态与多模态组合以及行为克隆基线，请对照原 PDF 查看逐条曲线。 下面总结用于评估”系统动力学系统性变化下下游策略性能鲁棒性”的环境扰动。 网格世界环境（grid_cliff、grid_sparse、grid_trap）。 通过在智能体的动作执行中引入随机性来扰动转移动力学：具体地，提高执行随机动作的概率 ，其中 对应确定性动力学。这些环境具有稀疏奖励以及悬崖或陷阱等惩罚区域，因此对动作噪声的鲁棒性尤为重要。 在网格实验中，所有方法在 时收敛到相同性能。这一行为直接源于随机动作的定义方式。设 是确定性策略 选中的动作，即 。在动作噪声下（概率 ），实际执行的策略变为
在 的网格环境中，令 会对所有动作 给出 ——等价于均匀随机策略。由于回报按”均匀策略取得 0.0”归一化，所有方法在 处都收敛到这个值。对于更大的 ，非意图动作获得比原始意图动作更高的概率质量，使确定性动作选择变得次优，因此我们把分析限制在 。 LunarLander-v3。 我们通过联合增大重力大小与风的强度来扰动动力学。具体地，重力参数在 中变化（默认 ），风力在 中变化（默认 0.0）。这些扰动产生越来越有挑战性的动力学：智能体既要缓解更强重力导致的快速下落，又要补偿风引起的横向漂移。 Acrobot-v1。 我们通过改变双摆两段连杆长度的比例来扰动系统。连杆间不对称性增大改变了系统的惯量与耦合，从而相对未扰动设定产生逐步不同且更具挑战性的动力学。 附录 F 额外定性结果（Additional Qualitative Results）本节给出所有网格环境的额外定性结果。[图 4]（grid_sparse，原文第 18 页）、[图 5]（grid_cliff，原文第 19 页）、[图 6]（grid_trap，原文第 20 页） 每幅都展示了同一推断奖励模型的两种可视化：
(a) 均值与方差的联合视觉编码（与图 1 一致）； (b) 对同一数据，均值与方差的分离视觉编码。
每幅图都由 网格上、来自 2 条示范、256 对成对比较、128 条评分 的推断结果组成；最右列展示组合全部反馈模态后的结果（各子图上方或图内标注了对应反馈模态与数据量，请对照原 PDF）。
需要说明的是，原文按反馈类型对推断出的奖励值做了线性归一化（这不会影响策略性能，因为最优策略诱导的行为对奖励函数的正缩放与常数平移不变，见 Ng et al., 1999）。
译后小结（供学习参考） 一句话概括：MAVRL 把”从人类反馈学奖励”统一成一个贝叶斯问题——共享一个潜在奖励函数 ，每种反馈（示范 D、偏好 P、评分 R、停止 S）都用自己的概率似然说话，全部放进一个 ELBO 里端到端训练，不再需要手工配损失权重。 方法骨架：奖励编码器 ＋ 辅助 Q 函数 （支持示范/停止这类需要价值估计的反馈）＋ 各类反馈的似然解码器 ＋ TD 正则把奖励与 Bellman 差分对齐。 四个似然：偏好＝Bradley–Terry；示范＝Boltzmann 理性策略；评分＝有序 logit（切点不等距）；停止＝关于终止时间的风险模型（几何分布，右删失）。 核心结论：(1) 组合反馈优于任何单模态；(2) 示范在稀疏奖励环境最强，评分在 CartPole 最好，偏好单用平庸但组合时贡献大，停止信号补充”次优性”信息；(3) 多类型联合推断对动力学扰动和大部分反馈误设（偏好/评分/停止）都很鲁棒，唯独示范通道被污染时仍是结构性短板；(4) 相对 MCMC 快约 30 倍、且能做连续控制，相对事后平均大幅更优。 阅读时建议对照原图：图 1 / 图 4–6 的”热力图”直观展示各类反馈留下的”不确定性模式”；图 2 / 图 3 的”鲁棒性曲线”直观展示组合反馈衰减更平缓。
本翻译由学习者整理发布，仅供学习交流；原文版权归作者所有。若用于正式引用，请引用原论文。

entry.title: 曾经，一场梦
entry.content: 现在是2026年10月18日晚上10点，我上洛谷看之前的文章。夜深忽梦少年事，真想梦啼妆泪红阑干，但是在图书馆，不行 这篇文章是 2024-03-30 22:52 写的，我已经无法完全的还原当时的心情，但我能体会到曾经的自己，那种遗憾，失落——这在最近一年多充斥着我的内心 当时的我没有那么强大的抗压能力，还是很脆弱的人，当然，也没我现在这么消沉 按照时间线，我当时应该刚分手？记不清了 正文 我一直记得我写过NOIP2024邮寄，然鹅没有找到，怪 于是因为过了这么久，我连NOIP整个过程已经记不清了，只记得退役之战虽然没有超长发挥，但也没有烂到体无完肤 然鹅比DGH低 考试之前我已经回归文化课了，考的时候心态也很放松，毕竟不指望这条路了，最后应该是155（我这记性真是绝了，这都记不住），去ZJ省三都不行，但陕西苟了一个省一（比分数线高了好几十分，可见SN有多菜） 不遗憾是不可能的，上竞赛谁又没有个梦呢，虽然是独木桥，但都曾认为自己会是闯过去的那一个，那些不切实际的幻想，终究是无根之萍 要相信概率，要知道差距 然鹅然鹅，即使是自己主动放弃，而且应该是明智的选择，偶尔亦会臆想那不切实际不可改变的结果 其实又何尝不是自己的原因，学习中（尤其是停课那段）效率有百分之几？水贴，水文的时间怕是比写题时间还长 偶尔也会做梦，如果当时会怎样，如果能重来会怎样，但不会怎样，不论是whk还是OI，我似乎都无法全心投入，甚至连投入一半都没有，这就是平庸的原因吧 学OI之前我一直觉得智商不低，但学OI之后被反复摩擦，智商人人都是250，或者说没到的都被唰下去了 总是习惯用智商弥补努力，但当智商不够了，我就寄了（whk中英语不也是这样） 我有时候很好奇为什么我初中不知道学信竞这么一回事，然鹅就算知道凭我初中那个鸟样也啥都干不了，所以结局早已注定 不充足的时间和懒惰的人，开头就预言了结尾 然鹅我也收获满满，我知道了编程是个什么东西，知道了很多大学可以打得比赛，拓宽眼界，我觉得这个东西在大学给我带来的帮助是不可估量的，我也认识了很多神犇，只能膜拜 大概还有些印象：前年七月，带着对未来的憧憬和不切实际的豪言壮志踏进机房，一年多后，带着遗憾与释然离场 留下了2.30k的提交，523的通过，30紫一黑，应该进过估值前500（呜呜，又记不清了），AT青名 虽然这些实在是不值一提，但确确实实是我存在的证明，我记性不好，很久之后，或许我只能从这些冰冷的数据中找到昔日热闹得模糊片段（我现在关于那些时光已经忘了好多，才过去不到半年啊） 突然想起来，拿了个省一也不是一点直接价值都没有，之前跟xcr聊的时候就说，可以拿省一坑蒙拐骗，卖点狗皮药膏，虽然有名的机构肯定是只要银牌之上的，但应该是有要省一的，这样就能赚点外快 不知不觉就写了800多字，想起昨天月考语文累死累活才扯了800多个字，今天到写的很顺溜，果然文由心生 OI生涯结束了（拢共也就一年半，跟那些学了好几年的大佬相比，实在不配叫生涯），但不会忘却，或许很多年以后，日薄西山之时，我还会想起这少年做过的梦，一起颓圮的时光，如同圆润的珍珠，穿在记忆的项链上 突然想起了很多很多每周六AT的紧张时刻放弃之后的4399时光一遍一遍调不出的RE WA 代码满屏绿之后的喜悦第一次切紫题严格次小生成树写了好几天那时候我才初学（大概四五个月？）我草我刚去看了一眼已经降蓝了我不管他就是紫题当时一步一步来，一行一行的调真的好厉害！！！对线段树特殊的感觉就是喜欢线段树暑假集训提单我只把他切完了以及一次次jcer与jcee的经历可惜还是有人没惨到好遗憾 死去的回忆突然攻击我 文章早就该完结了，但我总觉得话没说完 学OI让我看到了很多我连想都不敢想的东西，让我知道有些东西可望，也可即 但是能力配不上野心，看到却得不到，总是有些emo刚想了半天想用一个合适的词，单只想到了emo就是一种不可说的愁 刚学的时候我以为我最强的竞争对手就是DGH了，后来才发现有太多学的比我早还比我刻苦的人，真是那句话：当一个人比你小，还比你强，你就再也追不上他了 江哥小学爆杀33DAI，但我现在都没有一次超过33（我听课那会可是跟33说过我要吊打你那种豪言壮语呢） 突然发现我最后一次AT per1921,rank438,diff+108,将我从绿名送到青名，好吉利，这个句号很圆满 突然发现被机惨改成的洛谷名现在还没改回来，并且还改不了，乐 为什么我拿了两个一等奖还是绿名啊啊啊，好烦（虽然我知道为什么我是绿名，就差一点啊） 今天就写到这吧，哪天有感再写，或许明天，或许明年，或许这是最后一次打开洛谷，或许我的名字变灰并再也不会亮起

entry.title: agent对MAVRL论文的理解与总结
entry.content:
适用读者：准大二学生，数学上只学过高等数学与线性代数（没系统学概率与贝叶斯），深度学习学过神经网络 / CNN / RNN，略懂 Transformer。本文默认你不会概率论、贝叶斯与强化学习，遇到会用大白话补齐”最小必要知识”。 配套资源：本站另有《MAVRL论文全文中文翻译》（同目录下）。本文是”理解向”讲解，翻译稿是”原文对照”，两者配合使用。 原文信息：MAVRL: Learning Reward Functions from Multiple Feedback Types with Amortized Variational Inference，ICML 2026。作者：Raphaël Baur、Yannick Metz、Maria Gkoulta、Mennatallah El-Assady、Giorgia Ramponi、Thomas Kleine Buening（ETH Zurich / UZH）。代码：https://github.com/rabaur/mavrl
1. 这篇论文到底在干什么1.1 一个具体的场景假设你想训练一个机器人”整理书桌”。难题来了：你几乎不可能用数学公式写清楚”什么叫整理得好”——什么叫整齐？杯子放多正？书按什么顺序排？这些”微妙偏好、安全考虑、各种权衡”（论文原文 Introduction 第一句就在说这个）很难手工编码，而且规则写错一点点，就可能让机器人做出离谱甚至危险的行为。 但”评价行为”这件事你非常擅长，至少有四种方式：
反馈 你做的事 论文记号
示范 亲手做一遍给他看 D（Demonstrations）
偏好/比较 看两段行为，说”这段更好” P（Preferences）
评分 给它的表现打 1~5 分 R（Ratings）
停止信号 在它快闯祸时喊停 S（Stops）
这篇论文的核心主张就一句话：既然我写不出奖励函数，那就让算法从你这四种”评价”里，把奖励函数反推出来；而且这四种反馈不要分开训练，要放进同一个模型里联合推断，因为它们的”盲区”恰好互补。 1.2 为什么”反推奖励”要用概率和贝叶斯反推奖励时有一个无法回避的问题：数据永远不足以唯一确定奖励函数。比如看到专家往左走，可能是”左边奖励高”，也可能是”右边有惩罚”——两种解释都能解释数据。所以严谨的做法是：
不猜”奖励就是某一个函数”，而是维护”一堆可能的奖励函数，各自带一个概率”。
这就是”贝叶斯”的视角。让概率分布来表达”不确定”，是这个领域（以及整篇论文）的方法论基石。 1.3 论文的三个卖点（读完全文后再回来看） 统一：把四种反馈都写成”给定奖励，出现这种反馈的概率”（似然），从而放进同一个贝叶斯框架，方法上不需要针对每种反馈发明不同的损失函数； 省心：不需要手动调节”示范占多少权重、偏好占多少权重”——权重由数据和模型自动决定； 好用：组合反馈学出的奖励更准、下游策略更强、对扰动更鲁棒；还顺便给出奖励的”不确定性”作为可解释信号。
2. 最小知识包（读论文前必须补齐的概念）2.1 概率：只需要四件事你学过 CNN 分类，其实已经在用概率，只是没点破。这里只补四个最小概念：
随机变量：结果不确定的数。例：骰子点数 。 概率分布：每个取值有多可能。分类网络的 softmax 输出就是一个离散概率分布（所有类概率相加等于 1）。 期望 ：随机变量的”加权平均”。机器学习里所有损失函数，本质上都是”某种期望”的最小化——你训练网络时天天在用。 方差/标准差：衡量变量有多”飘”。论文里用它画”奖励不确定性图”（后面图 1 的模糊程度就是方差）。
2.2 贝叶斯公式：本文的心脏先用一个经典例子建立直觉：
某种病发病率 1%；检测准确率 99%（有病 → 99% 阳性，没病 → 99% 阴性）。某人检测为阳性，他真患病的概率是多少？ 答案约 50%，不是 99%。
直觉：10000 人里 99 个病人基本都被测出，但 9901 个健康人里有约 99 个被误报为阳性。阳性人群里真病人只占约一半。这个”反直觉的更新”，就是贝叶斯公式：
病阳性阳性病病阳性
病：先验（prior）——看到证据前的信念； 阳性 病：似然（likelihood）——假设”有病”，看到这个结果的概率； 病 阳性：后验（posterior）——看到证据后更新过的信念。
把这套语言翻译成论文：把”病”换成”奖励函数 ”，把”检测结果”换成”人类反馈数据 ”，就得到整篇论文的出发点：
：对奖励的先验（论文取标准正态，即”没有反馈时不做特别假设”）； ：似然——“假设奖励是 ，人类给出这堆反馈的概率”，论文第 4 节整节都在构造它； ：后验——看完反馈后对奖励的信念分布，这就是我们真正想要的东西。
贝叶斯式学习的哲学：学习 = 用数据把”先验信念”更新成”后验信念”。数据越多，后验越”尖”（越确定）——这正是论文图 1 里不确定性区域随反馈增多而缩小的原因。 2.3 卡住所有人的地方：那个积分算不出来公式写出来容易，用起来却有一个致命问题——分母：
它要对所有可能的奖励函数 积分。奖励函数是”从状态动作对到实数的映射”，有无穷多个。这个积分一般情况下没有解析解、也无法数值计算。 后果是：后验只能写成”正比于”的形式 ，分子算得动、分母算不动，导致后验无法归一化、无法真正使用。论文里管这叫”双重不可解（doubly intractable）”——名字唬人，本质就是”这个积分没法算”。 2.4 变分推断：算不出来，就找一个”模仿者”既然精确后验算不出来，换个思路：
找一个”算得动、好调参”的分布 ，让它尽量逼近真正的后验 。
就像模仿明星唱歌：不必懂声带解剖，只需要一个”能发声、可调节的嗓子（）”，反复听原唱（喂数据）调整自己，直到足够像。这里的”像”用 KL 散度衡量：
是自然对数；连续情形把求和换成积分即可，形式不用深究； 只需要记住一条：KL 散度非负，且越小代表两个分布越像（等于 0 当且仅当 ）。
直接最小化 依然算不动（里面还有那个积分）。但数学上可以证明，最小化它等价于最大化下面这个”算得动”的量：
第 ① 项：从 中抽奖励 ，看它平均能多好地解释反馈——逼着 往”能解释数据”的方向走； 第 ② 项： 不能离先验 太远——防止在数据少时乱猜（起正则作用）。
注意：第 ② 项里的 KL 是 对”先验”的（能算），不是对”后验”的（不能算）——这正是整个技巧的精妙之处：把一个算不动的目标，替换成一个可以优化的目标。这个”最大化 ELBO”的操作就叫变分推断（variational inference, VI）； 全称 Evidence Lower BOund（证据下界），因为它确实是 （”证据”）的一个下界。名字不用背，理解①②两条即可。 2.5 VAE、摊销与重参数化：为什么要”编码器”2.5.1 从自编码器到 VAE 自编码器：一个网络把输入压缩成小向量（编码器），再从小向量还原输入（解码器）。小向量 = 数据的”潜在表示”。 VAE（变分自编码器）：普通自编码器压出一个确定向量；VAE 压出的是一个分布（输出均值 和方差 ），再从这个分布里采样一个向量去解码。为什么要分布？两个原因：(1) 能表达不确定性；(2) 使潜在空间更连续、规整，采样出来的向量也”像真的”。
2.5.2 “摊销（amortized）”是什么意思传统的贝叶斯方法每来一份新数据，都要从头重新做一遍推断（慢、只能在小问题上用）。摊销的意思是：训练一个神经网络，让它学会”看一眼数据就直接输出后验大概长什么样”。训练好之后，新数据来了只需一次前向传播。把”每次现场重算”变成”训练时学一次、用的时候秒出”——这就是论文里的”奖励编码器“。 2.5.3 重参数化技巧（reparameterization trick）VAE / 本论文训练中有一道坎：要从 里采样 ，而”采样”这个操作本身不可导，梯度传不回去。技巧是：
先采一个与参数无关的标准噪声 ，再通过确定性公式算出 。于是随机性全部来自 ，而 变成普通的可导量——梯度可以正常反向传播。就这么简单，但它是一切”可训练的随机模型”的基石。 2.6 强化学习：只要 4 个名词这篇论文不是”训练策略”，而是”学奖励”，但正文会用下面四个词，最小认识即可：
名词 记号 一句话解释
MDP
环境的”说明书”：状态、动作、转移、奖励、折扣因子
轨迹
一局游戏从开始到结束的完整过程
回报
这局所有奖励的折扣求和； 越小越”近视”
策略 / Q 函数 / 策略：看到状态 选动作 的概率（结构上≈分类器的 softmax）；：在 做 、之后都按最优策略走，能拿到的期望回报
读本文不需要会训练策略（DQN / PPO 那些）。只要知道”训练策略 = 顺着奖励函数去优化行为”即可。
3. 逐节精讲论文3.1 全文结构地图（第一遍阅读的导航）
论文章节 讲什么 难度 第一遍怎么读
Abstract / 1. Introduction 动机与贡献 ★ 必读，先建立直觉
2. Related Work 前人的做法及不足 ★★ 第一遍可略读
3. Preliminaries MDP、贝叶斯后验、ELBO 的记号 ★★★ 必读，对照本文第 2 章
4. Feedback-Specific Likelihoods 四种反馈各自写成概率模型 ★★★ 核心，逐段读
5. MAVRL（方法） 编码器 + 多解码器 + 一个目标 ★★★★ 核心，配合本文第 2.5 节
6. Experiments 三组实验回答三个问题 ★★ 读结论即可，别陷进数字
7. Conclusion 总结与局限 ★ 必读
Appendix A–F 实现、超参、补充实验 ★★★ 第一遍跳过
3.2 方法的核心：一个”潜变量 = 奖励”的多解码器 VAE3.2.1 用 VAE 打比方回忆 VAE：图片 → 编码器 → 潜变量 → 解码器 → 还原图片。 MAVRL 是同一个骨架，只是换了”演员”：
状态动作对 → 奖励编码器 → 潜变量 （奖励）→ 四个”解码器”（四种反馈的似然）→ 分别解释 偏好 / 示范 / 评分 / 停止 数据
VAE 的潜变量 = 图片的”压缩特征”；这里的潜变量 = 每个状态动作对上的奖励； VAE 的”还原图片”= 重建损失；这里的”还原” = 解释你给的人类反馈； VAE 的编码器输出分布；这里的编码器也一样：
翻译成人话：网络看到 ，不说”奖励 = 3.5”，而是说”奖励大概是 ，我不太确定，不确定程度是 ”。 大的地方 = 图 1 里模糊的地方； 小 = 清晰的地方。 此外还学一个辅助的 Q 函数 ——因为示范和停止两种反馈的似然要用到”这个动作有多好”（见 3.3）。 3.2.2 为什么这样做等于”自动调节权重”把 2.4 的 ELBO 改写成”多种反馈各贡献一项似然”，就得到论文的总目标（公式 4）：
对比单反馈的 ELBO，唯一区别是：原来的一项 ，变成四种反馈对数似然的求和。没有任何”示范权重 0.3、偏好权重 0.7”之类的超参数。为什么不需要？因为：
如果示范数据能提供很强的信号，示范那项似然的梯度就大、自然主导学习；如果评分噪声大、信息弱，它的贡献自动变小。权重是”学”出来的，不是”调”出来的。
这是本文相对此前工作（如 Mehta & Losey 2024 用加性损失项、靠采样率定权重）最本质的改进。 3.2.3 最后一项 是干什么的 是一个辅助正则项。奖励编码器说”这里的奖励是 ”，Q 函数说”这里的价值是 ”。两者不该各说各话——Bellman 方程告诉我们，奖励和 Q 值之间有关系：
直观上， 可以理解为”从 采取 、再过渡到 这一步所隐含的奖励”——Bellman 方程保证它应与真实奖励一致。 做的事就是：逼着编码器输出的 尽量等于 （用高斯对数似然衡量偏差）。直觉：奖励网络说的，要和 Q 网络隐含的奖励对得上，两个网络互相监督、共同进化。它让只用”比较类”反馈（偏好、评分）时，模型也能学到合理的 Q 值，从而支撑示范/停止这类需要 Q 的似然。 3.3 四种反馈 = 四种概率模型（论文第 4 节）论文最优雅的地方：把四种反馈全部写成”给定奖励 ，出现这条反馈的概率“（似然）。一旦都成了概率，就能统一丢进 3.2 的框架。逐个来看。 3.3.1 偏好 P（Preferences）：Bradley–Terry 模型把两条轨迹的奖励代入 softmax：
等价写法： ，即 sigmoid。 比 高越多，”1 比 2 好”的概率越接近 1。 是逆温度： 大 → 判断果断； 小 → 经常”乱选”（标注噪声大）。
能提供：轨迹之间的相对好坏； 盲区：只关心”谁高谁低”，不关心差多少；比较之外区域的绝对好坏它完全沉默； 代价：成对比较要很多样本才顶用（论文实验里单独用偏好表现一般，组合时贡献才大）。
3.3.2 示范 D（Demonstrations）：Boltzmann 理性策略假设专家”越好的动作越可能选”，单步建模为：
一整条专家轨迹的似然 = 把每一步的选择概率连乘：
直觉：如果奖励 能完美解释专家每一步为什么这么走，这条轨迹在 下的概率就很大。反过来，最大似然就是在找”最能解释专家行为”的奖励。
能提供：专家走过的路是”好的、该走的”（且低不确定性）； 盲区：专家没走过的区域一无所知——状态空间覆盖稀疏； 代价：需要先有一个 Q 函数（所以要有 ）；示范似然很快”饱和”，给太多条边际收益低（论文附录提到示范数设上限的原因）。
3.3.3 评分 R（Ratings）：有序 logit（序数回归）人打分时，心里先有一个”真实质量分” ，叠加一点判断噪声，然后看它落在哪两个”切点”之间，就给几分：
其中 是 logistic 累积分布函数（就是 sigmoid 的”积分版”），切点 刻画”几分到几分的分界线在哪”。
关键：评分是序数信息（”大概 3 分档”），不是绝对数值（”这条值 3.7”）。所以模型把切点也学出来，而不是把分数当回归目标直接拟合。切点也不必等距——人本来就不会用均匀刻度打分； 能提供：可靠识别”目标/高奖励状态”； 盲区：目标周围的地形（”奖励怎么过渡”）信息模糊。
3.3.4 停止信号 S（Stops）：基于遗憾的风险模型先定义”这一步犯了多少错”——本可做到的最好，减去你实际做的：
这就是遗憾（regret）。再把历史错误折扣累加（ 让旧错误逐渐被遗忘），得累积错误量。人在时刻 喊停的”风险率”：
错误积得越多， 越接近 1，越可能在 被喊停； 越大，监督者越”没耐心”。观测到”正好在 被停”的概率是几何分布：之前每一时刻都没停 这一时刻停了：
若全程没被停，叫右删失——统计上不浪费这条信息，仍用它”至少没被停这么久”来约束奖励。
能提供：精确圈出”危险 / 低奖励区域”（这是偏好、评分很难给的”负信息”）； 盲区：只告诉你”这里不能去”，不告诉你”那该去哪”。
3.3.5 为什么必须四种组合（论文最重要的直觉）把每种反馈的”信息画像”并排看：
反馈 它擅长确定什么 它留下的盲区
示范 D 专家走过的路线（低不确定） 没走过的区域全盲
偏好 P 两条轨迹间的相对好坏 绝对水平、非比较区域
评分 R 目标/高奖励状态本身 周围地形过渡
停止 S 危险/低奖励禁区 禁区之外该去哪
四种合起来 = 高奖励区（示范/评分）＋相对排序（偏好）＋禁区边界（停止），每个方向的不确定性都被压缩。这就是论文图 1（10×10 网格上奖励热力图）想表达的：前几列单一反馈各有各的”模糊带”，最后一列组合反馈的重建结果又清楚又锐利。 读图 1 的正确姿势：别盯数值，盯”模糊程度”——每一行的不确定区域（方差大的色块）是怎么分布的，最后一列又是怎么被四种反馈从不同方向”夹击”而变清晰的。这就是”互补性”的直观证据。 3.4 实验部分怎么读（别陷进数字）论文做实验的目的是回答三个问题，看实验时也按这三个问题来抓重点：
不同反馈是否性质上互补？（→ 图 1，上一节已讲） 互补性是否转化为下游策略性能与奖励精度？（→ 表 1、表 2、附录表 4） 多反馈学出的奖励是否更鲁棒？（→ 图 2/图 3、表 3/表 5）
3.4.1 评估口径先看懂（否则数字没有意义） 归一化回报：把策略的回报缩放到”真实奖励训练出的近似最优策略 = 100、完全随机策略 = 0”。所以超过 100 表示”学到的策略比用真实奖励训练的还好”（正常现象，见下）。 EPIC 距离（越低越好）：衡量”学到的奖励”与”真实奖励”相差多远，且对”只差一个常数平移/正缩放/基于势的塑形”的奖励自动视为等价——因为这类变换不影响最优行为。它回答的是”奖励本身学得准不准”，与策略性能互补。 所有结果都在 个随机种子上取平均。
3.4.2 三个必须记住的结论结论一：组合 > 任何单模态（表 1）。 “四种反馈的组合”在 6 个环境中的 4 个取得最好或接近最好（归一化回报与 EPIC 距离双重指标）。注意表 1 里组合列超过 100（如 LunarLander 的 105.6、104.5），这不是 bug：真实奖励训练的”近似最优策略”只是 DQN/PPO 调出来的近似值，学到的奖励有时恰好让策略探索出更稳的行为。 结论二：没有万能单模态。 示范在稀疏奖励环境最强（grid_sparse、LunarLander 里接近满分甚至超 100），因为示范直接展示了”目标在哪”；评分在 CartPole 最好；偏好单独用一般般、组合时贡献大。“哪种反馈最好”取决于环境——这正是必须组合的理由。 结论三：组合更鲁棒。 两组实验：
对”环境变了”鲁棒（图 2/图 3）：奖励学好后冻结，然后扰动环境（给动作加噪声、改变 Acrobot 摆杆长度、给 LunarLander 加重力和风），只重训策略。结果：组合反馈训练出的策略性能衰减更平缓，单模态和模仿学习（BC）快速崩溃。 对”反馈本身被污染”鲁棒（表 3/表 5）：故意把某一类反馈弄坏（比如让标注者乱比较、给评分加高斯噪声、误校准停止倾向），再训练。结果：污染偏好/评分/停止三种之一时，组合模型能保留 ≥90% 的性能——其他通道把坏消息”补”了回来；但污染示范时组合也只剩 0.38~0.50——因为示范是信息最强的通道，它错了别的救不回来。
这最后一个细节特别能体现论文的诚实：它不吹”我们全场景无敌”，而是明确指出示范是”结构性薄弱点”。读论文要学这种态度。
3.4.3 两个基线对比（表 2）说明了什么 MCMC（非摊销的贝叶斯后验采样）：后验推断的”金标准”，慢。MAVRL 用约 1/30 的计算量达到相当或更好的性能，而且不需要内循环反复解 MDP，所以能上连续控制环境（MCMC 上不了）。 事后平均（分别训练各反馈的奖励模型再平均）：MAVRL 完胜。原因：独立训练的各模型奖励尺度和”塑形”各不相同，直接平均是”鸡同鸭讲”；联合推断则让它们共享一个奖励，天然对齐。
3.4.4 附录里值得知道的两件事（第一遍可跳过） 等预算实验（附录 C）：为了排除”组合好只是因为数据总量大”，论文把总反馈数固定（N=64 或 256），用贝叶斯优化决定怎么分给各模态。结论：连续控制环境组合依然占优；表格网格上单模态在”满预算”时也能赢——说明”组合的价值有多大”与环境的信息结构有关。 反馈是怎么造的（附录 A.2）：所有”人类反馈”其实是用 Boltzmann 理性策略 + 噪声参数模拟出来的（真实人类反馈留作未来工作）。理解这一点很重要——它既是本文的局限（合成反馈 ≠ 真人反馈），也解释了为什么能精确控制 、噪声等参数做可控实验。
4. 这篇论文和你已知的东西有什么关系4.1 它和 RLHF / ChatGPT 对齐是”近亲”你懂 Transformer，那一定听说过 RLHF（人类反馈强化学习）。ChatGPT 对齐的三段式是：SFT → 训练奖励模型（RM）→ PPO 优化。其中 RM 的训练主要就是 Bradley–Terry 偏好模型（本文 3.3.1 那个 sigmoid 式子，就是 OpenAI 那篇 “Deep RL from Human Preferences” 和 InstructGPT 里 RM 损失的同款）。 所以学这篇论文你实际上在学：
“如何从人类反馈中可靠地学一个奖励/打分函数” ——这是当今大模型对齐、机器人学习共同的核心问题。
MAVRL 与典型 RLHF 奖励模型的两点差别（值得对比着理解）：
RLHF 通常只用”偏好”一种反馈；MAVRL 研究”多种反馈怎么联合用”； RLHF 的 RM 输出一个确定的标量；MAVRL 输出一个分布（含不确定性）。
4.2 它和你学过的网络的对应关系
你熟悉的 论文里的 关系
编码器提取特征 奖励编码器 都是”输入 → 表示”的网络；只是论文输出的是分布参数
softmax 分类头 偏好/示范似然 Bradley–Terry、Boltzmann 策略本质都是 softmax
交叉熵损失 似然项的负对数 极大似然 = 最小化负对数似然，就是交叉熵的连续版
反向传播 重参数化技巧 为了让”随机采样”也能反传，先采噪声再算
正则化（如 weight decay） KL 项 都是防止过拟合的手段
L1/L2 辅助损失 TD 正则 都是”让两个预测对齐”的多任务技巧
4.3 它和 AVRIL / VAE 的血缘本文方法直接建立在 AVRIL（Chan & van der Schaar, 2021，”可扩展贝叶斯逆强化学习”）之上。AVRIL = “摊销变分推断 + 从示范学奖励”；MAVRL = “把 AVRIL 的单一示范似然，换成一组（示范/偏好/评分/停止）反馈似然，其余骨架不动”。
所以如果你想真正”看透”这篇论文，第二遍时把 AVRIL 原文找来对照读，收获会很大——你能清楚地看到作者”改了什么、没改什么”。
5. 常见疑问 QA（读的时候最容易卡住的点）Q1：评分已经是”打分”了，为什么不直接当回归目标训练？因为人的分数是”档位”不是”温度计”。同一个”4 分”，A 标注者眼里可能是 3.2，B 眼里是 4.8。强行当回归会逼模型去拟合标注者的主观刻度；而有序 logit 只假设”分越高 = 效用越高”，把”每个档的边界（切点）”也学出来，鲁棒得多。这也是原文反复强调”评分只提供序数信息”的原因。 Q2：停止信号这么”省事”（就是喊停），真的有用吗？有用，而且提供的是其他反馈给不了的负信息。示范说”走这里”，停止说”别去那里”——很多安全关键区域恰恰只能用”别去”来表达（你很难示范”错误路线”给机器人看）。论文实验里，含停止信号的组合普遍优于不含的（例如 grid_sparse 上 100.0 vs 示范单独的 95.0）。 Q3：为什么要费劲学”奖励的分布”，直接学个确定性奖励不行吗？第一，学分布是贝叶斯推断的自然产物（后验本来就是分布）；第二，不确定性有用——论文用它做”可解释性”（哪里没搞清楚一目了然），未来还能用它做”主动学习”（专门去问那些不确定的地方，论文在 Limitations 里明确把这个列为 future work）。 Q4：正文里的 PDR、PDRS 这些符号怎么这么乱？原论文用数学花体排印反馈记号，PDF 里看着像一串字母（PDR 常被用来指”全部反馈的组合”）。你只需要记住本文统一约定：P=偏好、D=示范、R=评分、S=停止，组合记号照原文保留，具体指哪几个以原图表为准即可。 Q5：为什么说”不用手动配权重”？梯度会自动平衡吗？严格说，权重是由数据量和似然形状共同决定的：信息强、样本多的反馈，其对数似然项的梯度贡献自然大。但这不等于”完全免费”——它有个前提：各种反馈的似然都被正确建模（噪声参数 、切点 、 要合理）。所以论文把”似然噪声参数”和”正则系数 ”分开讨论：前者是模型的一部分（可选作潜变量推断），后者才需要调，且性能对它们不敏感。 Q6：KL(q‖p) 不是对称的，为什么用这个方向而不是 KL(p‖q)？这是变分推断的一个经典细节：KL(q‖p) 会”惩罚 q 在 p 概率低处给概率”，导致 q 偏向”集中”（mode-seeking）；KL(p‖q) 则偏向”铺开覆盖 p 的所有可能”（mean-seeking）。工程上 KL(q‖p) 计算只需要能从 q 采样，天然适配”优化一个可采样的 q”，所以被采用。第一遍知道”方向不同、行为略不同”就够了。 Q7：我需要先会推导 ELBO 才能读懂论文吗？不需要。第一遍只需要接受两个事实：(1) 最大化 ELBO ≈ 最小化 q 与后验的 KL；(2) ELBO = “解释数据的期望” − “离先验的 KL”。推导留到二刷（且只需要会变分法基础 + Jensen 不等式）。
6. 按周学习路线（配套《MAVRL论文全文中文翻译》使用） 原则：只补到能读懂本文的程度，不要陷入”系统学完概率论+RL”的完美主义。每周末能回答”本章自测”即算过关。
📅 第 1 周：概率底子（每天 1~2 小时） 目标：随机变量、分布、期望/方差、条件概率与贝叶斯公式、最大似然。 方法：先看 3Blue1Brown《贝叶斯定理》 视频（建立直觉），再翻一遍学校《概率论》教材前 4 章。 自测：独立把本文 2.2 的”患病检测”例子算明白，并解释为什么”阳性≠99% 患病”。
📅 第 2 周：RL 名词 + 第一次读正文前半 目标：看懂论文第 3、4 节。 方法：看 李宏毅《强化学习基础》前 4 讲（只听懂 MDP/策略/回报/Q 的概念即可）；然后逐句读翻译稿第 3、4 节，对照本文第 2、3.3 节。 自测：能默写并解释四种反馈各自似然的”一句话直觉”与”盲区”。
📅 第 3 周：攻克 VAE / 变分推断（最硬的一周） 目标：看懂论文第 5 节，即公式 (4)。 方法：看 B 站”变分自编码器 VAE 从零推导” + 李宏毅 VAE 一讲；重点吃透：编码器输出分布、重参数化、ELBO 两项含义。 自测：向同学解释”为什么 ELBO 第一项让 q 解释数据、第二项把 q 拉向先验”。
📅 第 4 周：精读 + 写博客沉淀 通读论文正文（附录可跳），重点看图 1（不确定性模式）与表 1。 建议产出：像本文这样，把”四种反馈的盲区”画成四张小图再叠加，或写一篇自己的复述笔记发到博客。 挑战项：翻作者仓库 https://github.com/rabaur/mavrl 的损失函数代码，把公式 (4) 和代码行对应上——代码是最好的理解校验。
📅 可选进阶（暑假） 读 VAE 原文：Kingma & Welling, Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes； 读本文前身：Chan & van der Schaar, Scalable Bayesian Inverse RL（AVRIL），对比”改了什么”； 系统补 RL：Sutton & Barto《强化学习（第 2 版）》前 9 章，或周志华《机器学习》西瓜书的强化学习章。
7. 读完请自测（能答上 80% 就算真的读懂了） 用你自己的话（不许看笔记）解释：为什么后验 算不出来？变分推断是怎么绕过去的？ ELBO 的两项分别起什么作用？为什么第二项的 KL 是对先验而不是对后验？ 四种反馈各自的似然模型分别是什么？各举一个”它独有的、别的反馈给不了”的信息。 “摊销”是什么意思？为什么它能省掉内循环 MDP 求解？ 为什么”组合反馈”不需要手动调跨模态权重？什么情况下这个说法会不成立（提示：看论文 Limitations 与”示范被污染”实验）？ 实验里”归一化回报超过 100”正常吗？为什么？ MAVRL 和 RLHF 的奖励模型、和 VAE、和 AVRIL 各是什么关系？ 如果让你给这篇论文挑一个最值得做的 future work，你会选什么？为什么？（提示：论文自己列了三个）
写在最后：这篇论文对本科生来说属于”跳一跳才够得着”的难度，读不懂不是你的问题，是前置知识还没到位。按路线补完第 3 周，再回头看公式 (4)，你会觉得它”不过如此”——因为它的思想真的只有一句话：把四种反馈都写成概率，放进同一个贝叶斯目标里联合推断。 本文为个人学习笔记，公式与表述以原论文为准。原文见本站《MAVRL论文全文中文翻译》所附信息。

entry.title: MAVRL论文原文
entry.content:
原文信息 标题：MAVRL: Learning Reward Functions from Multiple Feedback Types with Amortized Variational Inference 作者：Raphaël Baur（ETH AI Center）、Yannick Metz、Maria Gkoulta、Mennatallah El-Assady、Giorgia Ramponi、Thomas Kleine Buening 机构：¹ ETH AI Center, ETH Zurich；² Department of Computer Science, ETH Zurich；³ Department of Informatics, University of Zurich 会议：Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026), Seoul, South Korea. PMLR 306, 2026. arXiv：2602.15206v2 ｜ 代码与模型：https://github.com/rabaur/mavrl ｜ 通讯作者：Raphaël Baur (raphael.baur@ai.ethz.ch)
阅读说明（本站整理，非论文原文）
本文是论文的英文原文全文（Abstract、正文第 1–7 节、Acknowledgments、Impact Statement、References、附录 A–F），不是翻译。内容由论文官方 LaTeX 源码（arXiv e-print，与 ICML 2026 camera-ready 一致）逐节转换而来，正文措辞未作改译。 公式已还原为 LaTeX 并交给 MathJax 渲染：行内公式用一对美元符号包裹，行间公式用两对美元符号包裹；原文的编号公式保留原编号 (1)–(4)，正文里的 “Eq. (1)” 等交叉引用也已按原文编号还原。 原文中的四种反馈类型在 PDF 里是小图标标签，这里统一记为 P = preferences（成对比较）、D = demonstrations（示范）、R = ratings（评分）、S = stops（停止信号），组合写法 PD / PR / PS / DR / DS / RS / PDRS 含义同理；带删除线的符号（P 等）表示该反馈通道被故意破坏（对应原文图标上的删除线），imitation 表示行为克隆（BC）基线。 图片请自行补充：每张图（图 1–6）的位置都留了占位块，块中标注了原文图片文件名（例如 figures/MARVLR_captioned_cropped.png），把图片放到站点图片目录后替换 > - 图片占位… 这一行即可（本站图片统一按 /img/xxx.png 引用）。 表格为原文表格的 Markdown 复刻：加粗 对应原文深灰底（该环境/列的最优），斜体 对应浅灰底（次优）；原表格用 \cmidrule 分组的子表头在 Markdown 中无法画分组线，因此改为在表头下方用一行标注分组（如 Singles / Pairs / All）。 原文脚注（正文中的上标注释）以引用块形式就近标注，并加”原文脚注”前缀以便区分。 参考文献列表由论文的 .bib 文件按被引条目生成，条目内容（作者、标题、出处、年份、链接）与原文一致，但排版格式（悬挂缩进、斜体期刊名缩略）与 PDF 不完全相同。
AbstractReward learning typically relies on a single feedback type or combines multiple feedback types using manually weighted loss terms. Currently, it remains unclear how to jointly learn reward functions from heterogeneous feedback types such as demonstrations, comparisons, ratings, and stops that provide qualitatively different signals. We address this challenge by formulating reward learning from multiple feedback types as Bayesian inference over a shared latent reward function, where each feedback type contributes information through an explicit likelihood. We introduce a scalable amortized variational inference approach that learns a shared reward encoder and feedback-specific likelihood decoders and is trained by optimizing a single evidence lower bound. Our approach avoids reducing feedback to a common intermediate representation and eliminates the need for manual loss balancing. Across discrete and continuous-control benchmarks, we show that jointly inferred reward posteriors outperform single-type baselines, exploit complementary information across feedback types, and yield policies that are more robust to environment perturbations. The inferred reward uncertainty further provides interpretable signals for analyzing model confidence and consistency across feedback types. 1. IntroductionDesigning reward functions that faithfully capture desired behavior is notoriously difficult. Even in well-specified environments, subtle preferences, safety considerations, and trade-offs are hard to encode by hand, and small misspecifications can lead to unintended or unsafe behavior (Abouelazm et al., 2024; Amodei et al., 2016; Gershman & Niv, 2015; Hendrycks et al., 2021; Knox et al., 2023). This challenge has motivated a broad line of work on reward learning, where reward functions are inferred from human feedback rather than specified explicitly. Such approaches are appealing because they allow domain experts to communicate intent through judgments or interventions that are often easier to provide than a complete formal specification. Human feedback about behavior, however, comes in many forms. Previous work has studied learning from demonstrations (Chan & van der Schaar, 2021; Ng et al., 2000), comparisons or preferences (Christiano et al., 2017; Wirth et al., 2016), scalar ratings (Knox & Stone, 2009), rankings (Brown et al., 2019; Myers et al., 2021), and interventions such as corrections or emergency stops (Ghosal et al., 2023; Hadfield-Menell et al., 2017; Losey et al., 2022), among others. Each feedback type provides only partial information about the underlying reward function: demonstrations offer sparse coverage of the state-action space and constrain rewards only along the expert behaviors; comparisons provide relative information about returns without fully specifying trade-offs beyond the compared alternatives; ratings only provide ordinal information about trajectories while discarding preference strength; and stops typically indicate unacceptable behavior without specifying what would have been optimal instead. As a result, relying on any single feedback type can leave aspects of the reward undetermined. These limitations highlight the need for learning from multiple feedback types, as different modalities can provide complementary information that resolves ambiguities left by any single source. Moreover, feedback types differ in availability, cost, and informativeness, making it important to understand how they relate to one another, how much information they provide, where they overlap, and when they conflict. Despite their complementary potential, learning reward functions jointly from heterogeneous feedback types remains challenging. Existing approaches either train separate reward models for each feedback type and combine them post hoc (Ibarz et al., 2018; Macuglia et al., 2025; Metz et al., 2025), or focus on a narrow subset of modalities, typically demonstrations and comparisons (Bıyık et al., 2022). Both strategies introduce significant challenges: post hoc aggregation raises questions about how to reconcile reward scales and uncertainties across feedback types, while collapsing diverse feedback into a single intermediate representation (such as preferences) can obscure modality-specific information and is not applicable to all forms of feedback. As a result, despite their complementary potential, jointly learning reward functions from multiple types of feedback remains difficult in practice. A more principled perspective is to view each feedback type as a probabilistic observation of a shared latent reward function. Under this formulation, learning from multiple feedback types naturally corresponds to Bayesian inference, where each feedback modality contributes information through its likelihood. Several frameworks formalize human feedback in this manner, for example, by modeling feedback as reward-rational choices from (possibly implicit) choice sets (Jeon et al., 2020). This likelihood-based formulation provides a conceptually unified treatment of heterogeneous feedback and makes explicit how different feedback types relate to the same underlying reward. However, exact Bayesian inference in this setting is generally intractable due to the need to marginalize over both feedback realizations and reward functions. To address these challenges, we introduce a scalable amortized variational inference approach for learning reward functions from multiple feedback types. Building on prior work on scalable Bayesian inverse reinforcement learning (Chan & van der Schaar, 2021), our method learns a shared variational reward representation together with feedback-specific likelihood models and is trained by optimizing a single evidence lower bound. Contributions. Concretely, our contributions are as follows:
We introduce a unified Bayesian formulation for learning reward functions from multiple feedback types, where each feedback modality contributes information through an explicit likelihood and no manual loss balancing is required (Section 4). We propose a scalable amortized variational inference algorithm that jointly learns a shared reward representation together with feedback-specific likelihood models (Section 5). We empirically demonstrate that jointly learning from multiple feedback types exploits complementary information, improves reward recovery and policy robustness, and yields interpretable reward uncertainty across a range of reinforcement learning benchmarks (Section 6).
2. Related WorkReward Learning. Reward learning seeks to infer reward functions from human feedback when explicit reward specification is impractical (Abbeel & Ng, 2004; Christiano et al., 2017; Ng et al., 2000). Early work focused on inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) from demonstrations, assuming expert trajectories arise from (approximately) optimal behavior under an unknown reward (Abbeel & Ng, 2004; Ng et al., 2000). More recently, preference-based reinforcement learning has gained prominence, particularly through applications in language modeling, where humans compare agent trajectory segments and reward models are trained using the Bradley-Terry model or related probabilistic choice formulations (Christiano et al., 2017; Ouyang et al., 2022).
原文脚注：Code and trained models are available at https://github.com/rabaur/mavrl.
Beyond demonstrations and preferences, a variety of other feedback types have been explored, including corrections (Bajcsy et al., 2017; Losey et al., 2022), rankings (Brown et al., 2020; Myers et al., 2021), and emergency stops (Hadfield-Menell et al., 2017). Each feedback paradigm introduces its own modeling assumptions and loss functions, and is typically studied in isolation. A unifying perspective was proposed by Jeon et al. (2020), who showed that many feedback types can be interpreted as reward-rational choices from (possibly implicit) choice sets. While this framework provides a common probabilistic interpretation of feedback, it does not by itself yield a scalable method for jointly learning from heterogeneous feedback sources. Approximate Inference for Bayesian IRL. Closely related to our work is the literature on scalable Bayesian IRL. Bayesian IRL poses reward learning from demonstrations as posterior inference, but early methods relied on MCMC or other sampling-based inference methods, limiting their applicability to small tasks (Ramachandran & Amir, 2007; Rothkopf & Dimitrakakis, 2011). To address this, Chan & van der Schaar (2021) proposed AVRIL, which applies amortized variational inference to Bayesian IRL by jointly learning a variational reward encoder and a demonstration likelihood decoder. This formulation enables efficient posterior inference without repeatedly solving a reinforcement learning problem in an inner loop and has been shown to scale to high-dimensional control as well as transformer-based reward models in language modeling (Cai et al., 2025). Other recent work has applied variational inference to preference learning to capture user-specific reward variation, but with a different objective than learning a shared reward function from multi-type feedback (Poddar et al., 2024). We build directly on the AVRIL framework by replacing its single demonstration likelihood with a set of feedback-specific likelihood models, while maintaining a single shared variational posterior over reward functions. This enables joint amortized inference from several feedback types without collapsing them into a common surrogate objective. Multi-Type Feedback. Compared to single-type reward learning, relatively little work has studied learning from multiple types of human feedback. Most existing efforts focus on demonstrations and preferences, and use demonstrations primarily as an initialization step before applying preference-based learning to further refine the policy and reward estimates (Bıyık et al., 2022; Ibarz et al., 2018; Macuglia et al., 2025; Palan et al., 2019). A small number of approaches attempt to incorporate more than two feedback types within a single learning procedure. Mehta & Losey (2024) integrate demonstrations, corrections, and preferences using the reward-rational choice framework in a robotics setting, but ultimately combine modalities through additive loss terms whose relative influence is fixed by design choices (e.g., sampling rates). Recent benchmark suites and evaluation platforms emphasize the practical relevance of heterogeneous feedback (Metz et al., 2023; Yuan et al., 2024), and existing large-scale studies evaluate combinations of feedback types using ensemble-style approaches (Metz et al., 2025). However, these approaches do not perform joint inference over a single reward function and instead rely on heuristics to reconcile different reward scales and uncertainties across feedback types. In contrast, our approach performs joint Bayesian inference over a shared reward function from multi-type feedback by integrating feedback-specific likelihoods within a single variational objective. 3. PreliminariesWe consider Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) with state space , action space , transition dynamics , ground-truth reward function , and discount factor . Both and may be discrete or continuous, and we do not assume access to the transition dynamics. Moreover, the reward function is assumed to be unobserved. The agent interacts with the MDP via a (possibly stochastic) stationary policy , which induces a distribution over trajectories in the MDP. We denote by the space of all stationary policies and with the space of all trajectories.
原文脚注：All definitions and results extend straightforwardly to finite-horizon MDPs by replacing the infinite discounted sum with a finite-horizon return. We adopt the infinite-horizon discounted formulation for notational convenience.
Given a reward function , the return of a trajectory is , and the expected return of a policy is . For a given reward function , we let denote the optimal action-value function. Bayesian Learning from Multi-Type Feedback. Given a set of multi-type human feedback , we are interested in learning a reward function. Concretely, we consider , where corresponds to feedback of type (e.g., preferences). Taking the Bayesian perspective, our goal is to infer a posterior distribution over the reward function given this data. Following this, we treat the reward function as a latent variable and consider
where is a prior over reward functions and is the likelihood of observing the multi-type feedback under . Crucially, the likelihood of observed feedback conditional on factorizes in a useful manner. As the observations are conditionally independent given the reward function, we can express the joint likelihood as . Hence, the multi-type feedback posterior satisfies . Amortized Variational Inference. Although elegant, equation (1) is generally doubly intractable: due to integrating over feedback choices in the likelihood and over all reward functions in the denominator. Variational inference (VI) addresses this intractability by approximating the posterior with a simpler variational distribution , whose parameters are learned by maximizing the evidence lower bound (ELBO):
The first term maximizes the expected data likelihood, and the second softly regularizes toward the prior . The Variational Autoencoder (VAE) framework (Kingma & Welling, 2014) made variational inference broadly applicable and scalable by representing the variational distribution as a neural network encoder that maps observations to latent variables , thereby amortizing posterior inference across data points. In addition, VAEs jointly learn a likelihood model , the decoder, which reconstructs the observed response from the latent representation .
原文脚注：Typically, in VAEs, the objective is to learn meaningful latent representations
through a reconstruction task, where .} This is enabled through the reparameterization trick, which expresses sampling as a deterministic transformation with , allowing gradients to flow through the encoder. 4. Feedback-Specific Likelihood ModelsWe define probabilistic likelihood models for each feedback type, which together induce the joint data likelihood in the Bayesian reward learning objective (Eq. (1)) and therefore determine the variational objective optimized by our algorithm. In this paper, we focus on preferences (pairwise comparisons), demonstrations, ratings, and stops, but the proposed framework and algorithm apply to any feedback type for which a probabilistic likelihood can be specified. Importantly, our method is agnostic to the particular choice of likelihood model and does not rely on shared intermediate representations or manual loss balancing across feedback types. Preferences (P). We here employ the commonly used Bradley-Terry model under which a trajectory is preferred over under the reward function with probability:
This formulation naturally extends to comparisons between trajectory segments, as in Christiano et al. (2017). The inverse temperature parameter controls the stochasticity of the preference judgments. Demonstrations (D). Expert demonstrations represent another commonly used form of feedback. Ramachandran & Amir (2007) and subsequent work, e.g., Chan & van der Schaar (2021); Rothkopf & Dimitrakakis (2011), model expert demonstrations through a Boltzmann-rational policy . We follow their modeling so that the likelihood of an expert trajectory under the reward function is given by
where the inverse temperature controls the degree of expert optimality. Ratings (R). Ratings provide ordinal feedback in which a human assigns a discrete score to a trajectory reflecting its perceived quality, analogous to Likert-scale judgments (Likert, 1932). We model this form of feedback using a standard ordinal regression framework, given by the ordered logit model (McCullagh, 1980). We assume that each trajectory induces an unobserved latent utility reflecting its quality under the reward function , corrupted by stochastic judgment noise. The reported rating is generated by discretizing this latent utility via an ordered set of cutpoints , such that a trajectory receives rating whenever its latent utility falls between and . Under this model, the likelihood of observing rating for trajectory is
where denotes the logistic cumulative distribution function. Importantly, this feedback modality is not equivalent to direct regression on the reward value, as it only provides ordinal information, but no absolute judgment. The cutpoints need not be evenly spaced, reflecting the fact that humans typically would not apply uniform or linear thresholds when mapping perceived quality to discrete ratings. Stops (S). Stop signals capture situations in which a human supervisor intervenes to terminate an agent’s behavior once its performance has degraded beyond an acceptable level. Such feedback is ubiquitous in practice, for example, as safety stops in robotics or human-in-the-loop control, yet has received little attention as a learning signal for reward or policy learning. Our framework naturally accommodates stop feedback by modeling it through an explicit likelihood over termination times. Let be the (random) time step at which the user intervenes. We model using a discrete-time hazard model in which the instantaneous hazard at time depends on the accumulated suboptimality of the trajectory up to that point. Concretely, we define the instantaneous suboptimality of action in state under reward as , and introduce a backward-looking discount factor that discounts earlier deviations. The resulting hazard function is given by
Here, the larger is, the more unforgiving the expert. We obtain the likelihood of observing a stop at time as the geometric distribution:
If no stop occurs within the segment, the observation is right-censored. Algorithm 1（原文 Algorithm 1，标题为 （MAVRL）Multi-Feedback Amortized Variational Reward Learning）

Additional Feedback Types. Other feedback types studied in the literature include rankings (Brown et al., 2019; Myers et al., 2021), corrections (Losey et al., 2022), and other forms of human intervention (Jeon et al., 2020). While we do not explicitly model these here, feedback-specific likelihoods can be derived analogously. Crucially, any such likelihood can be incorporated into our framework and algorithm without additional structural changes. We provide implementation details on feedback simulation in Section A.2. 5. MAVRL: Multi-Feedback Amortized Variational Reward LearningWe now present MAVRL, a general learning algorithm for Bayesian reward inference from multiple feedback types. The algorithm (Algorithm 1) instantiates the Bayesian objective introduced in Section 3 using amortized variational inference and directly leverages the feedback-specific likelihood models defined in Section 4.
[图 1] Visualizations of inferred reward functions from demonstrations, pairwise comparisons, or ratings on a grid_trap environment. The final column shows the result obtained when combining all feedback modalities.
图片占位（请自行插入原文图片）：figures/MARVLR_captioned_cropped.png
5.1. ObjectiveWe aim to learn a probabilistic reward model together with an auxiliary action-value function that supports feedback types defined in terms of state-action values. Specifically, we parameterize a conditional reward distribution
where and are parameterized as neural networks that map tuples to a distribution over local reward values. Sampling from this encoder induces a distribution over trajectory returns, which is used to evaluate feedback likelihoods. In addition, we learn an auxiliary action-value function , which is required by feedback types that depend on value estimates, as well as parameters associated with feedback-specific likelihood models when applicable, e.g., the cutpoints of the rating model. Crucially, the reward encoder itself is agnostic to the type and structure of feedback; all feedback-specific semantics are captured entirely by the corresponding likelihood functions. Learning follows directly from the evidence lower bound (ELBO) of the Bayesian reward learning problem. Given feedback datasets , where each contains observations of feedback type , the unified MAVRL objective to be maximized is given by
Here, denotes a generic feedback observation whose structure depends on the feedback type, such as a trajectory, a comparison, a scalar rating, or a termination time. Each feedback type contributes a likelihood term to the objective without requiring manual weighting or staged optimization. The final term enforces consistency between the inferred reward distribution and the auxiliary action-value function. Following Chan & van der Schaar (2021), we include a temporal-difference (TD) regularization term that encourages rewards predicted by the encoder to agree with the one-step Bellman differences implied by . To define this term, we leverage the trajectories associated with the observed feedback. Each feedback observation is grounded in one or more trajectories, from which we extract state-action transitions. Let denote such a transition tuple, where is the action taken in state . The corresponding TD target is defined as
We penalize deviations between this TD target and the reward predicted by the encoder by maximizing its log-likelihood under the encoder distribution,
where denotes the set of transitions extracted from the trajectories underlying the observed feedback. 5.2. Properties of MAVRLExtensibility. A central property of MAVRL is that it can use any form of human feedback for which a likelihood can be specified. Each feedback type contributes to the objective only through its likelihood term . Thus, adding a new feedback modality requires only defining its likelihood, without changing the reward encoder, auxiliary value function, or optimization. Unified Objective Without Cross-Modal Loss Balancing. MAVRL does not assume that different feedback modalities share a common intermediate representation or supervision signal besides the reward function. Feedback-specific likelihoods relate observations to the reward via different statistical relationships, such as action probabilities, return comparisons, ordinal thresholds, or cumulative regret. Because all feedback appears as log-likelihood terms in a single variational objective, the relative influence of each modality is determined by the data and feedback models, not by hand-tuned cross-modal weights. Thus, MAVRL removes the need to choose how much each feedback type should weigh in the reward estimator: For instance, with demonstration and preferences and known noise parameters, their relative weights in a combined loss or post-hoc ensemble are arbitrary in general MDPs. MAVRL avoids this issue entirely. Two parameter categories remain: Likelihood-specific noise parameters (e.g., Bradley–Terry temperature , rating cutpoints , and stop hazard parameters ) model annotator behavior and are grounded in established human-feedback models; they can optionally be treated as latent variables and inferred under behaviorally plausible priors. Regularization coefficients and control posterior regularization and reward–Q-value consistency; we tune them via standard model selection, and performance is stable over a broad range of values, with Q-value-based feedback (demonstrations and stops) requiring non-zero . Order-Invariant and Asynchronous Training. The training objective is agnostic to the order, frequency, and interleaving of feedback modalities. Mini-batches from each type-specific feedback dataset are sampled independently and can be combined arbitrarily during optimization. 6. ExperimentsWe evaluate MAVRL across a range of environments and feedback configurations to answer three questions:
((i)) how different feedback types qualitatively complement one another when learning reward functions (Section 6.1), ((ii)) how this complementarity translates into downstream policy performance and reward fidelity (Section 6.2), ((iii)) whether rewards inferred from multi-type feedback lead to more robust behavior under environment perturbations or reward misspecification (Section 6.3).
Our experiments span both tabular grid-world domains and continuous-control benchmarks, and consider demonstrations, pairwise comparisons, ratings, and stop feedback both in isolation and in combination. Unless otherwise stated, all methods are trained under a fixed feedback budget per environment, with identical numbers of feedback samples allocated to each modality to enable fair comparison. Let , , , and denote the numbers of preferences, demonstrations, ratings, and stop signals, respectively. In the grid-world environments, we set , , and . In Acrobot-v1 and CartPole-v1, we set , , and . In LunarLander-v3, we set , and . 6.1. Feedback Types Complement One AnotherIn Figure 1, we visualize reward estimates learned with MAVRL based on different individual feedback types and their combination in a grid-world environment. We report both the learned mean reward estimate and its corresponding uncertainty, quantified by the variance. Additional examples can be found in Section F. We find that each feedback type induces a characteristic pattern in the inferred reward and uncertainty estimates. Demonstrations yield low-uncertainty reward estimates along expert trajectories, but leave large regions of the state space underdetermined. Pairwise preferences provide broader coverage, but can assign a high reward to frequently visited intermediate states that are not globally optimal. Ratings reliably identify the goal state, but offer limited information about the surrounding reward landscape. Stop feedback strongly constrains unsafe or low-reward regions, while providing relatively little guidance on desirable behavior beyond avoidance. Illustrating the complementary nature of different types of feedback, these limitations are mitigated when they are combined. Our reward model, trained on combined feedback, can reconstruct the original ground-truth reward function with high fidelity and reliably identify both high- and low-reward states. 6.2. EPIC distances (bottom, lower is better) measure the divergence between learned and ground-truth rewards. We evaluate the downstream policy performance of different feedback combinations across a range of grid-world and continuous-control environments in Table 1. For each combination, we optimize a policy w.r.t. the learned reward estimate and report the policy’s total return w.r.t. the ground-truth reward function. All results are averaged over runs, and the returns are linearly scaled per environment so that corresponds to an approximately optimal policy trained on the ground-truth reward and corresponds to the return of a uniformly random policy. Hence, values exceeding indicate that the learned policy outperforms the policy trained on the ground-truth reward. While these normalized metrics capture downstream policy performance, they do not globally reflect reward recovery. To assess this, we also report EPIC distance (Gleave et al., 2021), which is zero for reward functions that are equivalent up to potential-based shaping, positive scaling, and constant shifts. We report EPIC distance only for tabular environments, where exact reward comparisons are feasible. Combining all feedback types yields the strongest overall performance. Overall, PDRS performs strongly across environments, achieving either the best or near-best performance in four out of six environments, with the exception of Acrobot-v1 and LunarLander-v3. This supports our central hypothesis that MAVRL is capable of leveraging complementary information captured in different feedback types. No single-type baseline dominates across all environments. Perhaps unsurprisingly, demonstrations (D) excel in sparse reward settings, such as grid_sparse (95.0) and LunarLander-v3 (115.7), while ratings (R) perform best in CartPole-v1 (100) among the single feedback type approaches. Preferences (P) show relatively modest performance as a standalone modality, yet contribute substantially when combined with others, consistent with prior findings that pairwise comparisons require large quantities to achieve competitive performance (Christiano et al., 2017). Stop feedback complements other feedback. In several environments, combinations involving stop feedback (PS, DS, RS) generally outperform their non-stop counterparts. For instance, in grid_sparse, DS (100.0) improves over D alone (95.0), and RS (70.6) similarly improves over R (58.8). This suggests that stop signals provide valuable information about the suboptimality of trajectories that is otherwise difficult to obtain from other feedback. EPIC distance reveals reward recovery quality beyond policy performance. In the three tabular environments where EPIC is computed PDRS attains the lowest (grid_cliff: ; grid_trap: ) or second-lowest (grid_sparse: ) EPIC distance. Discrepancies between EPIC and performance only occur on grid_sparse, where PR reaches the lowest EPIC () but only intermediate policy performance (), indicating that faithful reward recovery and high downstream performance, while not strictly equivalent, are jointly achieved by combining all feedback modalities. MAVRL is both effective and efficient relative to non-variational baselines. Table 2 compares MAVRL against two natural alternatives: MCMC, a non-amortized Bayesian reward learning method representing the gold standard for posterior inference, and Post-Hoc Reward Averaging, a non-variational heuristic that combines independently trained reward estimates through ensemble averaging (cf. Metz et al., 2025). Against MCMC, MAVRL achieves comparable or superior performance at roughly lower compute on grid environments and, unlike MCMC, does not require an inner-loop MDP solve, making it tractable on continuous-control settings where MCMC is not. Against Post-Hoc Averaging, MAVRL substantially outperforms naïve ensembling across all environments, indicating that independently trained reward models conflate signals with different scales and shaping and miss the cross-modal complementarity that joint inference captures. Gains persist under matched feedback budgets. To check whether the improvements from combining feedback types reflect genuine complementarity rather than larger total supervision, we conducted an equal-budget ablation with fixed total samples allocated across modalities via Bayesian optimization (Appendix C, Table 4). On continuous-control benchmarks, combinations consistently match or outperform the strongest single modality, with PDRS among the top performers. On the tabular grids, a single informative modality at full budget often beats fragmented multi-modality allocations, and pairs such as DR or PR emerge as the strongest combinations. Overall, combining feedback yields genuine cross-modal complementarity, with the benefit of including a given modality depending on its informativeness in the target environment.

We evaluate the robustness of reward functions inferred using MAVRL along two complementary axes: (i) robustness to shifts in environment dynamics at deployment, and (ii) robustness to noise and misspecification in the feedback used at training time. In both settings, reward models are trained once in the nominal configuration, then held fixed while policies are retrained without further reward adaptation, isolating the effect of reward quality from policy optimization. We compare individual feedback modalities, their combination (PDRS), and a behavioral cloning baseline (imitation). Full experimental details and results for all feedback combinations are provided in Section E. Multi-type feedback degrades more gracefully under dynamics perturbations. We perturb the transition dynamics of each environment after reward learning: increased action stochasticity in grid_cliff and grid_trap, structural changes to the system dynamics in Acrobot-v1, and shifts in gravity and wind in LunarLander-v3. Figure 2 shows the performance under these perturbations. In grid-environments, policies trained on rewards inferred from multiple feedback types degrade more gracefully under perturbations than those trained from individual feedback modalities or imitation alone. While downstream performance of combined feedback still degrades more gracefully than the imitation baseline, single-modality performance of, e.g., D, exceeds it, consistent with the unperturbed setting. In the grid-world setting, increasing action stochasticity causes imitation and single-feedback reward models such as D, R, and P to deteriorate rapidly, whereas rewards learned from combined feedback maintain higher mean returns. A similar pattern is observed in Acrobot-v1, where structural changes to the system dynamics disproportionately affect the imitated policy and the single-feedback reward models, while combined feedback yields consistently more stable performance across perturbation levels. In LunarLander-v3, perturbations to gravity and wind severely degrade the performance of imitation. In contrast, MAVRL, especially when trained with multi-type feedback (PDRS) and demonstration feedback (D), remains significantly more robust under increasingly challenging dynamics.

Multi-type feedback compensates for most misspecified modalities. Next, we test whether the multi-type advantage extends to corruption of the feedback signal itself, under the same fixed allocation feedback budget as in Section 6.2. We apply four misspecifications, individually or jointly: underestimated labeler noisiness for preferences () and demonstrations (), additive Gaussian noise on rating utilities, and miscalibrated stop propensity. Results for grid_cliff and grid_sparse are shown in Table 3; the same pattern holds on grid_trap (Table 5). Two observations stand out. First, for three of the four corruptions (preferences, ratings, and stops) PDRS retains of its well-specified performance, while the corresponding single-modality baselines collapse to ratios as low as . This suggests a strong compensation effect: Joint inference over multiple feedback types absorbs corruption from one source rather than propagating it. Second, the exception is demonstrations: corrupting them drives PDRS to ratios of –, and corrupting all four channels simultaneously reaches roughly the same level (–). The worst-case degradation of PDRS is therefore bottlenecked by the demonstration channel rather than compounded across channels. Overall, the multi-type benefit extends to upstream corruption in three of four feedback channels, with demonstrations remaining the structural weak point. 7. ConclusionWe framed reward learning from multiple feedback types as Bayesian inference over a shared latent reward function, where each feedback modality contributes through an explicit likelihood, and proposed MAVRL, a scalable amortized variational inference algorithm that optimizes a single unified objective. Empirically, we found that different feedback types induce distinct reward and uncertainty structures, and jointly inferring rewards from multiple modalities can exploit their complementary strengths, improving reward recovery, downstream policy performance, and robustness. Limitations. Our evaluation is limited to simulated environments, which, while allowing controlled analysis of different feedback types, do not capture the full complexity of real-world tasks. In addition, we rely on synthetically generating feedback, and applying MAVRL to real human feedback, which may exhibit systematic biases, inconsistencies, or context-dependent judgments, remains an important direction for future work. Finally, while our framework infers reward uncertainty, we do not yet exploit this uncertainty for guiding feedback collection, leaving active learning of heterogeneous feedback as a promising avenue for future work. A. Implementation DetailsA.1. Model ArchitectureThe reward encoder and Q-value estimator were implemented as two-layer MLPs with Leaky ReLU activations. For grid environments, we used learning rate , batch size 32, and state-only rewards . For control tasks (CartPole-v1, Acrobot-v1, LunarLander-v3), we used learning rate , batch size 128, and state-action rewards . All models were trained using AdamW with gradient clipping (max norm 1.0) (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019). The reward encoder parameterizes a Gaussian posterior with a standard normal prior, trained via the reparameterization trick. Expert reference policies were trained with StableBaseline3’s DQN implementation (all except LunarLander-v3) and PPO implementation (LunarLander-v3) (Raffin et al., 2021). Hyperparameter optimization. For each environment and feedback combination, hyperparameters are tuned with Optuna’s multivariate TPE sampler (constant\_liar=True, 20 startup trials) (Akiba et al., 2019). Each trial trains the model under a sampled configuration across multiple seeds and is scored by the chosen validation metric. The joint search space covers:
Loss weights and , log-uniform in ; Reward-encoder width: hidden units per layer for grids, for control tasks; Reward-model optimizer: learning rate (log-uniform ), batch size ( for grids, for control); For LunarLander-v3, the PPO retraining hyperparameters (learning rate, clip range, entropy/value coefficients, GAE-, gradient-norm bound, discount, rollout length, mini-batches, epochs) are searched jointly with the reward-model parameters.
We run this tuning under two feedback-allocation modes:
Equal-budget (Dirichlet) mode: a fixed total feedback budget is split across the active modalities via a flat-Dirichlet allocation suggested by Optuna. Per-modality caps (e.g., or demonstrations for grids/control, since demonstration likelihoods saturate quickly) are enforced by clipping the Dirichlet proportions and redistributing the excess mass. Fixed-allocation mode: each modality is assigned a prescribed sample count and only the optimization hyperparameters above are searched. This is used to characterize each modality’s contribution at a useful, comparable budget without confounding it with allocation choices.
The same tuning protocol (sampler, search space, seeds-per-trial, validation metric) is applied uniformly to all methods within an environment so reported numbers reflect best-of-search performance under matched compute. Model and training code was implemented with PyTorch (Paszke et al., 2019). A.2. Feedback SimulationWe simulate human feedback from trajectories collected by rolling out Boltzmann-rational policies with temperature parameter . Below we describe the generation process for each feedback type. Preferences. We extract random segments of fixed length from collected trajectories. For each pair of segments , we compute their normalized returns and generate a preference according to the Bradley-Terry model:where denotes the logistic sigmoid and controls preference rationality. The observed preference is sampled as a Bernoulli random variable with this probability. We choose , segment length , for grids and for all other environments, trajectory rationality for grids (uniform policy), for all other environments. Demonstrations. Expert demonstrations are generated by rolling out a Boltzmann-rational policy , where denotes the optimal Q-function. The demonstration rationality controls the degree of expert optimality. We choose for grids, for all remaining environments. Ratings. We extract random segments from trajectories and compute their normalized returns. Cutpoints are placed at the -th percentiles of the per-step segment returns. Ratings are then sampled stochastically under a cumulative-logit model, , which yields approximately balanced categories. Typical parameters: categories, segment length (grids, all other environments), trajectory rationality (grids, Acrobot-v1 and CartPole-v1, LunarLander-v3 respectively). Stops. We simulate stop feedback using a discrete-time hazard model based on cumulative regret. For a trajectory segment, we compute the instantaneous regret at each time step as and maintain a discounted cumulative regret:where is the regret discount factor controlling how quickly past suboptimality is “forgotten”. The hazard rate (probability of stopping at time given no prior stop) is: The sensitivity parameter is calibrated from the data as , where is a scaling constant and is a reference regret level (typically the 50th percentile of maximum cumulative regrets across segments). Larger yields more aggressive stopping behavior. Stop times are sampled sequentially: at each time step , we sample a stop event with probability . If no stop occurs within the segment, the observation is right-censored. Parameters: , regret discount , reference percentile , segment length (grids, all remaining environments), trajectory rationality . B. Hardware and Computational ResourcesDue to the large number of evaluated configurations in Section 6, individual reward model training and evaluation runs were distributed on a SLURM-managed institutional cluster, with each worker allocated 4 CPU cores and 8 GB of RAM. Due to the small size of the reward encoder and Q-value estimator networks, no GPU acceleration was required. For the final experiments, the total compute consumption amounted to approximately CPU-hours. We note that an individual reward model training run takes approximately 2 minutes for the grid environments and about 15 minutes for all other environments on a single machine, with most of the computation time spent on retraining a policy using the inferred reward function for evaluation. C. Equal Budget ResultsFor each environment we fix a single cumulative feedback budget shared across all 11 modality subsets considered in the equal-budget table: each of the four feedback types alone (P, D, R, S), all six pairwise combinations, and the full combination of all four (PDRS). The budget is samples for the three tabular grids (grid_cliff, grid_sparse, grid_trap), Acrobot-v1, and CartPole-v1, and samples for LunarLander-v3. For every (environment, modality subset) pair, we run a separate Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) search that jointly tunes (i) the proportion of allocated to each active feedback type and (ii) the reward-model training hyperparameters (encoder size, learning rate, batch size, importance-weighting toggle, KL weight, TD weight); for non-tabular environments the search additionally tunes the downstream PPO retraining hyperparameters. Each trial trains the reward model under random seeds for tabular environments and for non-tabular environments, and is scored by the per-seed mean of normalized discounted return (tabular) or mean episodic return (non-tabular); we run between and trials per study. The best-trial reward-model checkpoints are the ones used in all downstream transfer and misspecification experiments reported in this paper.

E. Additional Transfer Results and Detailed Perturbation DescriptionTransfer performance results for all feedback combinations are shown in Figure 3. We now summarize the environmental perturbations used to evaluate the robustness of downstream policy performance under systematic changes in environment dynamics. Grid-World Environments (grid_cliff, grid_sparse, grid_trap). For the grid-world environments, we perturb the transition dynamics by introducing stochasticity in the agent’s action execution. Specifically, we increase the probability of taking a random action , where corresponds to deterministic dynamics. These environments feature sparse rewards and punishing regions such as cliffs or traps, making robustness to action noise particularly important. In the grid-world experiments, all methods converge to the same performance as . This behavior follows directly from how random actions are defined. Let denote the action selected by a deterministic policy , such that . Under action noise with probability , the executed policy becomes
In the grid environments with , setting yields for all actions , which is equivalent to a uniform random policy. Since returns are normalized such that the uniform policy achieves a value of , all methods converge to this value at . For larger values of , unintended actions receive higher probability mass than the originally intended action, rendering deterministic action selection suboptimal. We therefore restrict our analysis to . LunarLander-v3. For LunarLander-v3, we perturb the dynamics by jointly increasing the magnitude of gravity and the strength of wind. Concretely, we vary the gravity parameter in , with default value , and the wind power in , with default value . These perturbations induce increasingly challenging dynamics that require the agent to mitigate rapid descents caused by stronger gravity while compensating for lateral drift induced by wind. Acrobot-v1. For Acrobot-v1, we perturb the system by varying the ratio between the two link lengths of the double pendulum. Increasing asymmetry between the links alters the inertia and coupling of the system, resulting in progressively different and more challenging dynamics compared to the unperturbed setting.
[图 3] Normalized mean returns ( ) of policies trained on rewards inferred by each method under three dynamics perturbation scenarios. Reward models and baselines are trained in the unperturbed setting and remain fixed throughout the variations.Returns are normalized such that corresponds to the performance of an approximately optimal policy trained on the ground-truth reward in the unperturbed setting and, analogously, corresponds to the performance of a uniformly random policy. Error bars denote standard error. (a) and (b) Increasing environmental stochasticity in grid_cliff and grid_trap. (c) Increasing ratio between pendulum handle lengths in Acrobot-v1. (d) Increasing gravity and wind-power in LunarLander-v3. 子图占位（请自行插入原文图片）：
(a) grid_cliff —— figures/transfer_grid_cliff_full.pdf (b) grid_trap —— figures/transfer_grid_trap_full.pdf (c) Acrobot-v1 —— figures/transfer_acrobot_full.png (d) LunarLander-v3 —— figures/transfer_lander_full.png
F. Additional Qualitative ResultsIn the following section, we present additional qualitative results for all grid environments. Figure 4, Figure 5, and Figure 6 each show two visualizations of the same inferred reward models: (a) a joint visual encoding of mean and variance, consistent with Figure 1, and (b) a separate visual encoding of mean and variance. Note that we linearly normalize the inferred reward values per feedback type. This would not affect policy performance, since the induced behavior of the optimal policy is invariant to positive scaling and constant shifts of the reward function (Ng et al., 1999).
[图 4] grid_sparse: Visualizations of inferred reward functions from demonstrations, pairwise comparisons, or ratings on a grid_sparse environment. The final column shows the result obtained when combining all feedback modalities.(a) Joint visual encoding of mean and variance. (b) Separate visual encoding of mean and variance for the same data. 子图占位（请自行插入原文图片）：

The final column shows the result obtained when combining all feedback modalities.(a) Joint visual encoding of mean and variance. (b) Separate visual encoding of mean and variance for the same data. 子图占位（请自行插入原文图片）：

The final column shows the result obtained when combining all feedback modalities.(a) Joint visual encoding of mean and variance.
